page.title: Virtual Events Platform Comparison Guide
page.description: Learn how to choose between self-serve streaming, webinar tools, and enterprise event suites. Compare cost models, technical requirements, and production needs.
page.h1: How to compare virtual events platform options
page.definition: Virtual events platforms are software tools used to host digital gatherings, ranging from simple streaming studios to complex enterprise event suites. Choosing the right platform requires matching your specific audience outcome, technical requirements, and budget to the correct category of software and production support.
page.quick_answer: Select a platform based on your event format: use self-serve tools for simple broadcasts, webinar software for moderated sessions, or enterprise suites for large-scale conferences. Always separate your software purchase from your production requirements.

sections.h2: What are the different types of virtual event platforms?

blocks.p: Platforms fall into three distinct categories based on complexity and control. You must decide if you need a simple broadcast tool, a structured webinar environment, or a full-scale digital conference experience.

sections.h2: How much do virtual event platforms cost?

blocks.p: Pricing depends entirely on your scale and how the vendor structures their licensing. There are three primary cost models to evaluate during your procurement process.

ul: Per-host licences sized by attendee capacity, such as Zoom Webinars
Self-serve monthly plans, such as StreamYard or Livestorm
Annual contracts quoted by sales, such as ON24, Cvent, Bizzabo, or Goldcast

sections.h2: What is the difference between platform and production?

blocks.p: Platform and production are two separate purchases that require different budgets and expertise. The platform is the software used to host the event, while production refers to the human crew and technical equipment required to run it.

ol: Platform: The software subscription, registration engine, and digital venue
Production: The crew, cameras, encoder, run of show, and backup stream
Deliverables: Branded slide templates, lower thirds, live producer, and Q&A moderation
Rehearsal: One full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before the event

sections.h2: How do I manage the event workstreams?

blocks.p: Successful events require dividing tasks into specific workstreams with clear ownership. West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations to manage these complexities.

sections.h2: What is the timeline for a virtual event?

blocks.p: Lead times vary significantly depending on the complexity of the format. You should plan your logistics well in advance to ensure technical stability and speaker readiness.

ul: Webinars: Three to four weeks of lead time
Summits or online conferences: Six to eight weeks of lead time
Hybrid conferences: Six to eight weeks to lock venue AV and the platform
Technical check: Sixty minutes before going live

faq.q: How much does professional event production cost?
faq.a: Moderated webinars typically range from $2,500 to $7,500 per production. For larger formats like executive summits, online conferences, and hybrid productions, costs range from $10,000 to $50,000 and above. These figures represent production services, not the software platform subscription itself.

faq.q: Can I use my existing software for a virtual event?
faq.a: Yes, events can be produced on the platform you already use, such as Zoom Webinars, Microsoft Teams, ON24 or StreamYard. The key is ensuring your chosen platform supports the specific engagement features, such as Q&A or breakout rooms, required for your event format.

faq.q: What happens if the internet or software fails during a live event?
faq.a: A professional production includes a backup stream to mitigate technical risks. Part of a robust run of show involves having a producer manage the platform and ensuring a technical check is completed sixty minutes before going live to identify potential points of failure.

faq.q: When should I send the event replay to attendees?
faq.a: You should send the replay within 24 to 48 hours of the event finishing. This timing ensures that attendees still remember the content and are more likely to engage with the recording or move into the next stage of your marketing funnel.
